Disregard for Human Life: Critics cite devastating real-world outcomes, such as a U.S. strike that killed over 200 civilians at an Iranian elementary school. It has led the world on Wolbachia, a common bacterium that infects roughly half of all insect species and does not harm humans or other warm-blooded animals. Releasing Wolbachia-carrying Aedes mosquitoes ended local dengue transmission in Townsville, in tropical northern Australia, not far from dengue-endemic Indonesia. The Times has covered this well. The billboards I saw in southern Florida promote genetically engineered mosquitoes, which is a different strategy.

Florida should not downplay dengue. I grew up in India, where malaria was the infection everyone knew and dengue was rarely mentioned. In about 25 years that reversed. Aedes thrives in warming, polluted cities and breeds in discarded tires, bottles and caps. It has spread dengue nationwide and put many young people in the ICU. Most people there now accept it as permanent.

Australia’s template could work in the parts of the U.S. closest to the tropics.

comments.name: J
comments.body: Some climate skeptics point to previous periods of Earth's drastic warming (and cooling).  This should alarm, not please, them.  Climate + natural systems have been fortuitously stable since the last ice age--about 10,000 years and not coincidentally when agriculture was invented and human civilization took hold.  It's an eye-blink against a backdrop of geologic time.  The 5 previous mass extinctions in the fossil record were all caused by climate disruption (one triggered by an asteroid).  The difference?  They were natural.  This one is man-made.  If five of your children died of natural fever, you wouldn't purposefully induce a fever in the sixth, would you?  You would try hard to keep the temperature down for as long as you could.  We're doing the opposite.  Wait long enough, sure, and the world will be too hot (or too cold) again.  But if our absurdly recent species wants a longish run, we might do well to preserve what we have and be instinctively cautious about chemically disrupting it.

Electricity is displacing fire as the foundation of human existence, we cannot survive without it. For the first time, with the telegraph and soon after the telephone, people could interact remotely in real time. It was the beginning of an evolutionary transition leading to the emergence of a new species of human in the Electric Age. Steven Reed Nelson, "Fire in a Wire: Electricity Enables Humans to Evolve Beyond Homo Sapiens."

They merely invented modern voice and data telephony and bequeathed the Unix operating system that is the basis of alternatives to Microsoft Windows. Does this book trace fiber-optic telephone cables from their introduction decades ago to now when they are replacing copper telephone wiring everywhere? The marvel is not that we each have a telephone; it is that each of our telephones can connect to every other telephone worldwide. Years ago, I heard on NPR Sir Edmund Hillary speaking to the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, when he said that his son phoned him yesterday — from the summit of Mount Everest.

I'm thinking back to the classics from my childhood like Dragon Ball, Sailor Moon, and Digimon; middle/high school shonen like Naruto and Inuyasha; all-time greats like Fullmetal Alchemist and Attack on Titan; and recent hits like Frieren and The Apothecary Diaries. These stories have almost nothing in common with each other—what they do share is the obvious care and attention of authors creating worlds and characters that deeply resonate with the audience. This isn't something that you can just focus-group and churn out of a corporate boardroom. RIP

comments.name: Chente
comments.body:
He gets a pass on the Cooke debacle; no one is infallible, especially under the circumstances. However, the Jackson incident was a terrible, inexcusable breach of journalistic ethics that had nothing to do with race. 

At the end of the day, all that journalists have is their word. Or put another way, their credibility, which includes trust and honesty. That word was broken. Unless Jackson changed his mind and agreed to go on the record, his comments should never have been published, no matter how vile they were. And make no mistake- what Jackson said was horrific. But journalism ethics, no matter how uncomfortable at times, exist for a reason. They should never be treated or viewed as situationally optional.

comments.body:
This is bleak. I know, I know - consumerism is a problem. But reading between the lines here in this article - the average shopper is feeling an enormous amount of stress and panic about their day to day budgets.

I have been pretty broke in my life, and for the readers out there who are looking for holiday gift-giving ideas that cost very, very little, here are some gifts I have given in the past when I have been hard up - hope it can help some of you this holiday season!:

- Writing handwritten, thoughtful letters to the people you love. You can share what you love about them and how they mean so much to you. Put a nice ribbon or bow on the letter envelope and it looks great under the Christmas tree.
- Cooking your loved one's very favorite meal. Your gift can be an invite on a nice little card that shows what the menu will be. Everyone loves a home cooked meal! Get some fresh bread and butter or a salad mix for an appetizer and make the entree - boom, you have a coursed dinner!
- Develop and frame a picture of one of their favorite memories. It is cheap to develop a picture at Walgreen's/CVS/Walmart, and you can thrift a nice frame.
-  The thrift store - find a nice flannel or scarf for under $5, launder it nicely, and fold it in some gift wrap.

The thought is what matters, and with a little care into how you present something, you can have an affordable gift that means a lot. You don't have to go in debt or go to an expensive store to make the holidays fun and memorable.

I think the rise in 'fancy' or "craft beverage" has contributed to much of the decline. And I'd like analysis of the amounts Gen Z spends on $8 lattes vs. alcohol. That's another thing that has changed - the rise of the pricey coffee drinks. I'm a millennial (40), we mostly had Starbucks and a few indie coffee shops here and there, but the drinks were fairly basic. We went out plenty but the alchol drinks were also fairy basic (cheap beer; cheap well drinks). Now there are far fewer basic bars and far more upscale places selling $16-20 mixed drinks as well as coffee shops selling $8-10 lattes. Coffee shops are PACKED with Gen Z. Same with food -- gone are the days of simple lunch spots, Applebees 1/2 price happy hours, and diners; now replaced with bougey dining that cost $20+ an entree. 

I think that has something to do with it - everything is so fancy and overpriced at all levels, that 20-somethings just can't afford to really partake. So they stay home. Or go out for one drink. Or they get a coffee 4x per week instead of binge drinking on weekends.

After moving to Maine in the late 80s and leaving an active dancing career in NYC, I lost touch with many independent choreographers I respected and wanted to work with, like Neil. I saw a performance in Portland, ME, in the late 80s, which was the last time I spoke to him. I enjoyed his dancing with Merce, which made me excited that he was choreographing for himself. I send condolences to him for the loss of his husband and his brother. The 80s were indeed extremely difficult with the AIDS epidemic, and I joined the dance community, going to memorials practically every week. We lost so many talented artists, and we each lost at least one person close to us before the meds came out. I was delighted to see this positive article about Neil & his dancers and get a bit caught up. Being older, I seldom get down to NYC. I'd love to see this new piece. I wish him all the best for continued success, health, and happiness wherever he can grasp it. 
Christine Philion-Dufour

comments.name: Jessica Hutauruk
comments.body: If I had the privilege to interview a veteran or service member, I would ask, "What motivates you to continue serving and fighting for your country, even when you know that some people do not fully appreciate the military, knowing that you are still putting your life on the line to protect their freedom and lives?" Hearing two completely different sides of society on the matter of the military constantly makes me wonder if we truly understand what service members in the military endure for our freedom. Throughout my life, I've witnessed tragedies happen in my country, and to think of the many lives we've lost to fight and protect our country is unimaginable. I have always wondered if veterans or service members hear about society underestimating their hard work and adversities they have been through for strangers that they don't know. Veteran day is coming up and it's important to understand we can have different view points that are occurring in our country today, but ultimately, veterans sacrificed their lives to protect our freedoms today.

comments.name: TL
comments.body: I agree with Mr. Craven, and truly believe that Veterans’ memories serve as a prime source of information about past conflicts and how they shape our understanding of possible solutions for current conflicts. Their memories are a first source to the horrors, friendships, and bonds created between man and nature, their stories are first takes that should be spread to further raise awareness about the environment of war so we can make critical decisions on how to address current world problems. It’s also through holidays, such as Veterans Day, Memorial Day, and even monuments that our society today can take time to think about relatives, friends, and people in their lives that have put forth a sacrifice that could have cost them or has cost them their life. In my opinion, we can best honor veterans by understanding their journey, talking to them about their experiences, and connecting with them, through hearing their stories, honoring their sacrifice, and acknowledging the effort they put into their service and for our community.

comments.body:
What if Megaspeed was not merely a customer, but an intermediary through which Nvidia chips, supplied via Aivres, ultimately reached China?

What if this happened with the full knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has actively advocated for access to the Chinese market?

And what if Trump knew about these arrangements while considering his family's financial interests in Nvidia and the broader AI industry?

These are hypothetical questions, not established facts. But the implications could be enormous.

While the Commerce Department investigated suspected chip smuggling, Nvidia lobbied to ease export restrictions. The investigation was subsequently transferred to the Justice Department, raising questions about the independence of enforcement.

Was this legitimate business, deliberate circumvention of export controls, or political protection?

Who knew what, when, and who ultimately profited?

Independent journalists must investigate the supply chain, financial transactions, lobbying contacts, and potential conflicts of interest.

Follow the chips. Follow the money. Follow the political connections.

Were national security laws enforced independently, or did powerful corporate and political interests influence the outcome?
